colossus

/kuh-LOSS-uhs/ - the stress falls on LOSS · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Colossus means a gigantic statue or thing.

Cut into the canyon wall, the sandstone colossus watched over the trade road for twelve centuries, its knees alone taller than the caravans passing beneath.

Example

When the dictator fell, the crowds went first to the steel colossus of him in Victory Square. It took three cranes and two days to bring the hundred-foot figure down, and its severed head, big as a delivery van, sat in the grass all winter.

Colossus outdoes 'statue' and even 'monument' by making size the whole point: from the Colossus of Rhodes onward, it names a figure so gigantic that people measure it in ship-masts and stories — and, by extension, any towering giant of its field.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

titan: A titan is a towering figure of power — a titan of industry, a tech titan. Borrowed from mythic giants, the word points at influence first and size second, and a titan is a person or force, never an object you could carve or cast. A colossus is, first of all, physically gigantic.

monolith: A monolith is a single huge block of stone — or an organization so massive and uniform it seems carved from one. Either way it is one solid, faceless mass. A colossus is a shaped figure: gigantic, but sculpted into a form people crane their necks to take in.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

figurine: a statue small enough to hold in one hand

miniature: a tiny version of something usually far larger

Where it sits · how overwhelming the physical scale is — statue → monument → colossus

statue vs. colossus: A statue can be any size at all — a garden gnome qualifies — while a colossus is defined by overwhelming scale.

monument vs. colossus: A monument is built big enough to honor its subject, yet even a grand one stays within human measure; a colossus bursts past it, so vast that visitors gauge it in stories and ship-masts — which is why this ladder can end nowhere else.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — coloss

Root — coloss: a gigantic statue (Greek kolossos)

Suffix — -us

Suffix — -us: Latin noun ending

Put it together

Put it together: Coloss- (a gigantic statue) + -us (the Latin noun ending) = the giant figure itself. Greek kolossos named the enormous statues of the ancient world — above all the bronze Colossus of Rhodes — and the root still means 'gigantic' wherever English uses it.

Use the root in a new word: colossal

Use the root in a new word: colossal: Repaving every road in the county in a single summer was a colossal undertaking that emptied the budget.

Word Choice

vivid / literary

Colossus is the word when size itself inspires awe: a carved colossus, or a person or company that towers over a field like one. Its unit-mate behemoth looms with menace, a monster crowding everything near it; a colossus stands magnificent, a marvel to look up at. For a giant of myth-level influence, titan is the close cousin.
